summary: This standards-track document defines a TLV for IS-IS that records which router generated a purge. Purges currently carry no such information, so it is hard to find the source of problems. Because flooding does not change the purge contents, the TLV remains attached as the purge spreads.

eli5.summary: When a router deletes info from everyone's map, nobody knows who did it. This adds a signature to the deletion note so troublemakers can be found.

questions: how to find which router purged an is-is lsp
what is the is-is purge originator identification tlv
how do i find which router sent an is-is purge
subtitle: A small IS-IS extension that stamps each purge with the system ID of the router that created it.

tldr.problem: An IS-IS purge carries no information about which Intermediate System (IS) generated it, so operators cannot easily find the source of a bad or unexpected purge.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6232 defines the Purge Originator Identification (POI) TLV, code 13, which records the system ID of the IS that created the purge and, optionally, the system ID of the neighbor it was received from. It also lets the Dynamic hostname TLV ride along in purges.
tldr.outcome: Operators and developers can log where a purge came from. The RFC is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5301, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310 and is itself updated by RFC 8918.

today: RFC 6232 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2011. It updates RFC 5301, RFC 5304 and RFC 5310, and it has itself been updated by RFC 8918.

sections.title: Why Purges Need a Name Tag
sections.content:
IS-IS floods purges throughout an area no matter which IS started them. A purge is a link state PDU (LSP) that tells the other routers to remove old information. If an operator wants to investigate why a purge happened, the protocol gives no way to find out where it came from.

The RFC notes that field experience has shown several cases where an IS improperly generates a purge. These come from implementation deficiencies, or from implementations that predate ISO Technical Corrigendum 1 and generate a purge when they receive a corrupted LSP. This document adds a TLV to purges that records the system ID of the IS generating the purge.
sections.eli5: Imagine a class where anyone can shout 'erase the board!' and nobody sees who did it. It is hard to find out why the board keeps getting erased. A name tag on every shout fixes that.

sections.title: The Purge Originator Identification TLV
sections.content:
The POI TLV uses CODE 13. Its LENGTH is the total length of the value field. The value holds a one-octet count of system IDs (only the values 1 and 2 are defined), then the system ID of the IS that inserted the TLV, and optionally the system ID of the IS from which the purge was received.

The TLV SHOULD be found in all purges. It MUST NOT be found in LSPs with a non-zero Remaining Lifetime, so it only ever appears on purges and not on live LSPs.
sections.eli5: The tag has a small number saying how many names are on it (one or two), then the name of the router that wrote it and, sometimes, the name of the neighbor who passed it along.

sections.title: Who Adds the TLV
sections.content:
If an IS generates a purge, it SHOULD include the POI TLV with its own system ID. If an IS receives a purge that has no POI TLV, it SHOULD add one carrying both its own system ID and the system ID of the IS from which it received the purge.

This lets routers that receive purges log the originator or the upstream source. The RFC says this makes it much easier for a network administrator to locate the origin of a purge and so its cause, and that the TLV also helps developers in lab situations. Because normal LSP flooding does not change LSP contents, the TLV propagates along with the purge.
sections.eli5: The router that starts the purge signs it. If a purge shows up unsigned, the first router to notice signs it with its own name and the name of the neighbor who handed it over.

sections.title: Adding the Dynamic Hostname TLV
sections.content:
The RFC also extends the use of the Dynamic hostname TLV (type 137, from RFC 5301) to help identify the system that generated the purge. This TLV MAY be included in purges. Implementations SHOULD include one instance of it if the POI TLV is included, and only the local hostname should be inserted.

A hostname is easier for a person to recognize than a raw system ID.
sections.eli5: A router can also write its friendly name on the tag, because names are easier for people to read than ID numbers.

sections.title: Authentication and Mixed Networks
sections.content:
Using these extensions with authentication as defined in RFC 5304 or RFC 5310 will cause purges to be discarded by legacy systems that strictly conform to either of those RFCs. That may compromise the correctness and consistency of the routing database unless all ISs in the network support the extensions.

For that reason, all implementations in a domain that use authentication MUST be upgraded to receive the POI TLV before any IS is allowed to generate a purge with the POI TLV. Further interactions between the POI TLV, the Dynamic hostname TLV and the Authentication TLV are described in RFC 6233.
sections.eli5: If some routers do not understand the new tag, they may throw the whole message away. So every router must learn about the tag before anyone starts using it.

sections.title: The Code Point
sections.content: IANA assigned code point 13 for the Purge Originator Identification TLV in the IS-IS TLV Codepoints registry. The additional values for this TLV are IIH:n, LSP:y, SNP:n and Purge:y, meaning it is not carried in IS-IS hello PDUs or sequence number PDUs, but is allowed in LSPs and in purges.
sections.eli5: The tag was given its own official number, 13, so every router recognizes it the same way.
